paras: The threatened lynching at Lafayette, Alabama, took place in December 1881, when a crowd was reported going to the Lafayette jail to demand a Black prisoner accused of killing a merchant in Chambers County. A Montgomery dispatch said there was a "strong probability" that the man had been hanged, and papers from Savannah to Sacramento repeated the story, one of them as an accomplished lynching. No later report confirming or denying his death appears in the coverage.

According to the dispatch, dated Montgomery, December 9, a merchant in Chambers County was "called up by some negroes for alleged purchases" a few nights earlier and was struck down and killed when he opened his door. The Waco Daily Examiner's printing placed the killing "Four nights ago," or about December 5. The merchant's name appeared as W. McLann in Savannah, W. McCann or William McCann in Richmond, Chicago and Sacramento, and W. Norcourt in Waco, all in the same dispatch.

Suspicion fell on "certain negroes," and one man, once arrested, was reported to have confessed and led the arresting party to the place where the money was buried. A Portland brief described his confession more narrowly, as "participation" in the killing. He was held in the jail at Lafayette.

On the night of December 8, reports reached Montgomery that "a great crowd from the scene of the tragedy was going to the jail to demand the prisoner." On that basis alone the correspondent judged it probable that he had been hanged; the dispatch gave no account of the crowd reaching the jail or of any killing.
No report of an inquest, arrests, or any official action appears in the coverage, and none of the papers printed a follow-up on the prisoner's fate.

The story reached readers on December 10 almost entirely through the single Montgomery dispatch, printed in full in the Savannah Morning News, the Richmond Daily Dispatch, the Waco Daily Examiner, the Knoxville Daily Chronicle and the Dallas Daily Herald. Shorter versions ran the same day in the Chicago Daily Tribune, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Los Angeles Daily Herald, and the Warren Sheaf repeated it a week later with no new information. Southern papers filed it under crime news, as "Alabama Crimes" in Richmond and "Criminalities" in Waco, without editorial comment.

The story grew more certain as headline and summary writers condensed it. Savannah headed it "Threatened Lynchug in Alabama," while the Chicago Tribune called the prisoner "a Negro Murderer" and said he was "expected" to have been lynched. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union printed the dispatch as "Murder and Lynching" with the word "expected," yet its news summary in the same issue said flatly that "the murderer was lynched." The Los Angeles Daily Herald ran the item under a racial slur. Every version treated the confession as settling the prisoner's guilt.

The papers disagreed on whether the lynching had happened: the dispatch spoke of a "strong probability," the Chicago Tribune of an expectation, and the Portland Daily Press of a belief, while only the Sacramento summary line called it fact. Because that summary condensed a dispatch printed in the same issue with the hedged wording, it adds no independent evidence that the prisoner was killed.

reader.title: Threatened lynching at Lafayette, Alabama (1881)
bases: A crowd was reported going to the Lafayette jail to demand a Black prisoner accused of murder, with a "strong probability" that he had been hanged (A1, A5, A7).

Every report descends from one Montgomery dispatch that said only that the prisoner had probably been hanged because a "great crowd" was heading to the jail (A1, A5, A6); the one flat statement that he "was lynched" is a summary line whose own paper printed the dispatch as "expected" (A3, A4), and no report confirming a killing was found.
All twelve printings are versions of a single Montgomery dispatch of December 9 (A1, A5, A7), and no independent or later report was found.

accounts.label: Montgomery wire dispatch, December 9
accounts.gist: A merchant was killed by Black men who called him to his door; a suspect confessed and was jailed at Lafayette, and there was a "strong probability" he had been hanged, since a great crowd was going to the jail to demand him.

accounts.label: Condensed wire version
accounts.gist: The confessed man was lodged in Lafayette jail and "it is expected" he had been lynched, as a great crowd was seen on the way to the jail.

accounts.label: Newspaper summary lines
accounts.gist: One brief said it was "believed" he had been hung by a mob; another stated flatly that "the murderer was lynched."

framing.detail: Papers ran the Montgomery dispatch under crime-news heads such as "Alabama Crimes" and "Criminalities," treating the confession as settling guilt and the expected lynching without comment.

Headline writers hardened the story as it travelled: the Chicago Tribune called the prisoner "a Negro Murderer," the Sacramento Record-Union's summary said "the murderer was lynched," and the Los Angeles Herald used a slur.

conflicts.note: All are printings of the same dispatch, so these are most likely telegraph or typesetting variants of one name, not different men.
The flat statement is a summary line in the same Sacramento issue whose full dispatch said only "expected" (A3), so the dispatch's hedged wording is the better evidence.
The dispatch says the merchant was killed by several men ("some negroes") but that one confessed "the crime."

record_check.record: William McCann (killed, not the lynching victim); W. Norcourt (killed by the accused, not by the mob)
record_check.dossier: One merchant, not two: McLann, McCann and Norcourt are variant names in printings of the same dispatch. The person the crowd targeted was the unnamed Black prisoner.
Threatened; a killing was reported only as probable or expected, apart from one summary line, and was never confirmed.
The accused prisoner is called "a certain negro"; the merchant's race is not stated.
Merchant killed about December 5, 1881; crowd reported heading to the jail December 8.

record_check.record: said to have killed merchant William McCann
record_check.dossier: Accused of the killing and reported to have confessed and led captors to buried money; one brief says "participation."

info: Merchant killed "a few nights ago" (A1, A6, A7) or "Four nights ago" (A5) before the December 9 dispatch, i.e. about December 5, 1881; the crowd was reported heading to the jail in "last night's reports" (December 8).
Merchant killed at his home in Chambers County; the accused was jailed at Lafayette.

The target of the threatened lynching was an unnamed Black prisoner ("a certain negro") held at Lafayette; the merchant killed beforehand was named W. McLann, W. McCann, William McCann or W. Norcourt in different printings.
Accused of killing the merchant, who was struck down when he opened his door to "some negroes" calling about purchases; reported to have confessed and led his captors to buried money.
"a great crowd from the scene of the tragedy"; race and names not stated.
Unconfirmed: one possible (the prisoner), reported only as probable or expected except in one summary line.
